# Sima de los Huesos Hominins

## Site, Excavation, and Chronology

The Sima de los Huesos ("Pit of Bones") hominin assemblage represents one of the most significant and well-documented collections of Middle Pleistocene human fossils ever discovered , . Located deep within the Cueva Mayor-Cueva del Silo cave system in the Sierra de Atapuerca mountain range in Burgos, Spain, the site provides an unparalleled window into human life nearly half a million years ago , . Geographically, the chamber is situated approximately 600 meters from the main entrance of the cave system, accessible only via a complex network of tunnels and vertical drops, making systematic excavation a formidable challenge that has required decades of dedicated effort . The specific location of the bone deposit is at the bottom of a narrow, 13-meter-deep vertical shaft, which descends from an upper chamber known as the Sala de las Oseras (Cyclops Chamber) , . This extreme remoteness has been crucial to the exceptional preservation of the fossils, shielding them from surface weathering and much of the environmental disturbance that affects more exposed sites .

The discovery of the site by amateur cavers marked the beginning of a major paleoanthropological endeavor. The first human fossil was identified in 1976 by Trinidad Torres, a member of the Edelweiss Caving Club (ECC), who reported his findings to palaeontologist Emiliano Aguirre , , . Formal investigation began in 1978 under Aguirre's leadership, but systematic excavations commenced in earnest in 1984 after significant infrastructure was installed to make access feasible , . These annual, month-long campaigns, conducted continuously since 1984, have been led by a team of prominent researchers including Juan Luis Arsuaga, Eudald Carbonell, and José María Bermúdez de Castro, who succeeded Aguirre after his retirement in 1991 , . Over forty years of work have yielded a remarkable trove of over 7,000 hominin fossils, representing a minimum of 29 individuals , , . The site's importance is underscored by its designation as a UNESCO World Heritage site on November 30, 2000, alongside other Atapuerca sites .

The archaeological context of the Sima de los Huesos deposit is defined by its unique taphonomic signature. The hominin bones are embedded within a lithostratigraphic unit designated LU-6, a bone-bearing breccia composed of limestone blocks, mud, and sedimentary fill , . Detailed sedimentological analysis reveals that the deposit lacks fluvial features such as sorting, rounding, or lamination, which would be indicative of transport by water . Instead, the fracture patterns observed in the breccia are consistent with low-energy vertical fall and limited mudflow, strongly supporting a depositional mechanism where bodies fell directly into the pit from above rather than being carried there by rivers . This interpretation is further corroborated by paleomagnetic analysis of the illite-rich LU-6 sediment, which confirms it is younger than the Brunhes–Matuyama reversal (~780,000 years ago), placing it firmly within the current magnetic chron . The faunal association provides additional context; the chamber contains a vast number of bear bones, primarily from the extinct cave bear species *Ursus deningeri*, along with remains of other carnivores like the cave lion (*Panthera leo*) and wolf (*Canis lupus*) , . Stratigraphic relationships suggest that the hominins were deposited before the bears, possibly when the upper shaft collapsed, trapping both humans and animals inside .

The precise dating of the Sima de los Huesos hominins has been a central focus of research and a source of considerable debate, ultimately leading to a high-resolution chronology based on the convergence of multiple independent geochronological methods. Early estimates placed the age of the fossils between 400,000 and 500,000 years ago, with some studies suggesting a much older date of around 600,000 years , . For instance, a 2007 study by Bischoff et al. proposed an age of ~600 ka based on U-series dating, though this was contested by others , . However, a series of more advanced and integrated dating techniques have progressively refined this timeline, establishing a robust consensus. A landmark 2014 study by Arsuaga et al. synthesized data from uranium-series (U-series) dating of speleothems (cave formations) that formed on top of the crania, thermally transferred optically stimulated luminescence (TT-OSL) and post-infrared stimulated luminescence (pIR-IRSL) on quartz and feldspar grains within the sediment, electron spin resonance (ESR) dating of fossil teeth and sedimentary quartz, and paleomagnetism , . This multi-pronged approach, analyzed using a Bayesian age-depth model, constrained the age of the LU-6 unit to approximately 430,000 years ago, with a refined range of 410,000 to 460,000 years ago , , . This date is now widely accepted and superseded earlier broader estimates . The age places the Sima hominins squarely within Marine Isotope Stage (MIS) 12, a period of cool climate conditions , . This precise chronology is not only critical for understanding the site itself but also for its profound implications in human evolutionary theory, as it situates the population near the predicted time of the divergence between the Neanderthal and Denisovan lineages , . This convergence of evidence from disparate scientific fields illustrates the power of modern paleoanthropology to resolve long-standing questions of chronology, providing a firm temporal anchor for interpreting the biology and behavior of the Sima de los Huesos hominins.

## The Fossil Assemblage and Demography

The Sima de los Huesos fossil collection is extraordinary not only for its sheer volume—comprising over 7,000 individual bone fragments—but also for the remarkable completeness and quality of preservation of the material, which has enabled an unprecedentedly detailed reconstruction of a single, cohesive Middle Pleistocene human population , . The assemblage includes representatives of virtually all anatomical parts, from complete distal pedal phalanges to fragmentary skulls and postcranial elements, allowing for comprehensive morphological and biological analyses , . As of the latest assessments, the collection represents a minimum of 29 individuals, an update from the previous estimate of 28 , . This figure is based on extensive dentognathic reconstruction, including antimeric fitting of jaw fragments, staging of occlusal wear, and analysis of developmental markers like enamel hypoplasia, which accounts for damage inflicted by amateur cavers prior to formal excavation , . The sex ratio of the population is not significantly different from a 1:1 balance, correcting earlier suggestions of female predominance , . The remains span a wide range of ages, from preadolescents to individuals reaching advanced age, providing a rare snapshot of a closed-population demography , .

A detailed analysis of the age-at-death distribution reveals a striking mortality profile, often described as "catastrophic" or L-shaped, indicating a skewed population structure , . Among the 29 individuals, 12 were immature (41.4%), and another 12 were young adults (aged approximately 17–30 years, 41.4%), leaving only 4 middle-aged adults (13.8%) . This pattern suggests a population with a high rate of mortality among the young and a scarcity of individuals surviving to middle age. Further analysis of dental development shows a significant acceleration compared to modern humans; third molar (wisdom tooth) eruption occurred systematically 2.8 to 4.1 years earlier, with an average age of eruption estimated at 14–15 years, compared to approximately 18 years in contemporary human populations . This accelerated maturation is a distinctive feature of the Sima hominins and provides a key biochronological marker for identifying members of this population across different archaeological contexts. Beyond demography, the skeletal remains provide profound insights into the biology, pathology, and potential social behaviors of these ancient people. Their overall body plan is characterized by robustness and a "wide" bauplan, a plesiomorphic trait inherited from early hominin ancestors . Stature estimates for the population are comparable to those of modern human middle-latitude populations, with mean statures calculated at 174.4 cm for males and 161.9 cm for females based on talar measurements . Long-bone-based estimates confirm these robust modern human-like body proportions . However, despite this gracility in some aspects, the population exhibited a highly robust body plan overall, contrasting sharply with the more gracile build of modern humans . This is evident in features like broad pelves, long superior pubic rami, and broad lumbar transverse processes , . Body mass was slightly lower than that of later Neanderthals, and their encephalization quotient (EQ), a measure of relative brain size, was significantly lower than both Neanderthals and modern humans, suggesting that full Neanderthal-sized brains had not yet evolved in this population . This mosaic pattern of traits highlights the stepwise nature of Neanderthal evolution.

Perhaps the most poignant aspect of the Sima de los Huesos collection is the evidence of pathology and potential care for the infirm. One of the most remarkable discoveries is Cranium 14, the skull of an immature individual aged between 5 and 12.5 years at death . This individual suffered from severe lambdoid single suture craniosynostosis, a congenital condition where the lambdoid sutures of the skull fuse prematurely, causing severe deformity of the head and likely associated cognitive and motor disorders . The severity of the deformity, including pronounced cribra orbitalia (porous lesions on the eye sockets), was the most extreme seen in the entire Sima sample . The survival of this individual to a relatively advanced age implies that they received care from their conspecifics, offering a rare and powerful glimpse into the potential for compassion and social support within this Middle Pleistocene community . Another compelling case of pathological stress is found in the form of widespread healed antemortem cranial injuries. A comprehensive taphonomic study identified 57 distinct, circular, blunt-force trauma lesions across 17 of the 20 crania analyzed , . These lesions, which show clear signs of bone remodeling and healing, affected individuals of all ages and both sexes, indicating that the entire population was exposed to recurrent, nonfatal cranial impacts throughout their lives , . While the cause of these injuries is debated, interpretations range from accidental hazards of daily life to recurrent low-level interpersonal violence , . The presence of such a high frequency of healed injuries paints a picture of a challenging and potentially violent existence for these ancient people.

## Taxonomy and Anatomical Affinities

The taxonomic placement of the Sima de los Huesos hominins has been a subject of intense scholarly debate, fundamentally reshaping the understanding of human evolution in Europe during the Middle Pleistocene. For decades, fossils from this era, including those from Sima de los Huesos, were broadly classified under the species *Homo heidelbergensis*, a taxon envisioned as the last common ancestor of Neanderthals, Denisovans, and modern humans , . However, the wealth of new data from Atapuerca, combined with discoveries elsewhere, has led to a significant re-evaluation. The overwhelming consensus from morphological and genetic analyses is that the Sima hominins are best classified as early members of the Neanderthal lineage, rather than as *H. heidelbergensis* , . This conclusion is supported by a suite of derived traits that align them more closely with classic Neanderthals than with contemporaneous or earlier hominins like *Homo erectus* or *Homo naledi* , . The shift in classification was catalyzed by molecular divergence estimates that pointed to a split between Neanderthals and modern humans around 400,000 years ago, a timeframe that coincided with the age of the Sima fossils and made it difficult to place them within a basal *H. heidelbergensis* group .

Detailed anatomical analysis of the Sima crania provides strong evidence for their status as basal Neanderthals. One of the most definitive pieces of evidence comes from the morphology of the bony labyrinth (inner ear). Studies have shown that the semicircular canal proportions of the Sima hominins exhibit a derived pattern identical to that of Neanderthals—a relatively smaller posterior canal and a relatively larger lateral canal—which is distinct from the pattern seen in *Homo sapiens*, *H. ergaster/erectus*, and early hominins . Furthermore, the SH bony labyrinth is considered primitive relative to later Neanderthals, lacking certain derived features like a high sagittal labyrinthine index, which confirms their position as basal members of the Neanderthal clade rather than as *H. heidelbergensis* . Cranially, the Sima sample exhibits a characteristic mosaic of traits. They possess several derived Neanderthal features, particularly in the face and anterior vault, related to the masticatory apparatus, such as intensive frontal tooth wear, which suggests the use of the mouth as a 'third hand' for holding objects while working , . The supraorbital torus (brow ridge) is thick and torsioned, a feature also seen in early Neanderthals, although it lacks the fully arched profile of classic Neanderthals , . However, the braincase morphology retains more primitive characteristics, supporting the "accretion model" of Neanderthal evolution, which posits that facial modifications preceded significant changes in the neurocranium , , . Endocranial volumes vary considerably, with specimens ranging from 1,125 cm³ to 1,390 cm³, averaging around 1,232 cm³, which is less derived than the larger brains of later Neanderthals , , .

The dental remains from Sima de los Huesos constitute the largest Middle Pleistocene hominin dental assemblage ever recovered, comprising over 533 teeth . This extensive sample allows for a nuanced understanding of their dental evolution. The molars exhibit "almost morphological identity with European Neanderthals," displaying a high frequency of taurodontism (enlarged pulp chambers), a prevalence of approximately 75%, which links this Middle Pleistocene population morphologically to later Neanderthals , . The occlusal patterns of the upper first molars (M1s) also show a mosaic of traits, with some features matching *Homo neanderthalensis* while others align with *Homo sapiens*, highlighting the complexity of dental evolution and cautioning against simplistic taxonomic assignments based on isolated teeth . Interestingly, while the absolute and relative enamel thickness of SH molars is generally thick and plesiomorphic (primitive), similar to that of *Homo erectus* and modern humans, the enamel distribution pattern is derived and Neanderthal-like, with thicker enamel concentrated on the lingual cusps , . This dual signal—retaining ancestral enamel thickness while evolving a derived distribution—is a key piece of evidence supporting their position as early Neanderthals. A 2025 study further complicates the picture by noting intrapopulation variability in enamel thickness and cautioning against relying solely on this metric for taxonomy, as lower premolars show a more modern-human-like pattern while upper premolars are more Neanderthal-like .

Postcranially, the Sima hominins display a similarly mosaic pattern of Neanderthal apomorphies and primitive traits. The talus (ankle bone) is a key element of interest. The sample includes 17 talus specimens, all of which show complete fusion of the anterior and middle calcaneal articular surfaces—an autapomorphic trait shared with Neanderthals (present in 96% of the sample) but less common in both Pleistocene and recent *Homo sapiens* (present in 88.9% and 55-75% respectively) . The SH tali are also vertically shorter and have a broader lateral malleolar facet than all comparative samples, contributing to a broader, more robust foot morphology . Other postcranial elements, such as the pelvis, also show features consistent with the Neanderthal clade, such as a broad elliptical shape with a wide sacrum and long pubic rami . However, the population also retains primitive traits, such as large femoral heads, which are characteristic of the Middle Pleistocene . This mosaic evolution in the postcranium, where some features are shared with Neanderthals while others are retained from earlier ancestors, underscores the gradual and piecemeal nature of the transition to the classic Neanderthal phenotype. The combination of these cranial, dental, and postcranial features solidifies the classification of the Sima de los Huesos hominins as a pivotal link in the evolutionary chain leading to Neanderthals.

## Ancient DNA and the Mitonuclear Paradox

The advent of ancient DNA (aDNA) technology has revolutionized the study of the Sima de los Huesos hominins, introducing a profound paradox that has become central to modern discussions of archaic human evolution. In 2014, a groundbreaking study published in *Nature* successfully sequenced mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) from a 400,000-year-old femur from the site, representing the oldest hominin genetic material ever retrieved at the time , . The results were astonishing: the mtDNA from the Sima hominin formed a clade with the Denisovan lineage, an archaic human group known primarily from fossils found in Siberia, and was more distantly related to Neanderthals , , . This finding was deeply contradictory because the skeletal anatomy of the Sima fossils is unambiguously Neanderthal-like, exhibiting numerous derived traits that are hallmarks of the Neanderthal lineage , . This discrepancy, known as mitonuclear discordance, presented a major puzzle: how could a population with Neanderthal-like bones carry Denisovan-like mtDNA? The initial surprise was compounded by the fact that the Sima hominins were dated to approximately 430,000 years ago, placing them at a critical juncture in human evolution, near the hypothesized time of the Neanderthal-Denisovan split , .

To resolve this enigma, scientists turned to the even more challenging task of extracting ancient nuclear DNA (nDNA), which carries the vast majority of an organism's genetic information and provides a more reliable phylogenetic signal. In 2016, another landmark study, also published in *Nature*, announced the successful retrieval and sequencing of nDNA from two Sima hominin specimens , . The results were definitive: the nDNA analysis confirmed that the Sima hominins are indeed part of the Neanderthal evolutionary lineage, showing a closer phylogenetic relationship to Neanderthals than to Denisovans , , . This finding resolved the paradox by demonstrating that the surprising mtDNA result did not represent the ancestral state of the population but rather a subsequent event in their history. The scientific consensus that emerged from this research is that the Sima population, while belonging to the early Neanderthal lineage, must have experienced gene flow from another archaic hominin group, likely one related to Denisovans or perhaps an unknown population, which introduced the Denisovan-like mtDNA lineage into their gene pool , , . This later mtDNA replacement event explains why the maternal lineages diverged from the main Neanderthal branch before the split between Neanderthals and Denisovans, while the rest of their genome remained firmly rooted in the Neanderthal clade.

This mitonuclear discordance has had far-reaching implications for calibrating the timelines of human evolution. By confirming that the Sima hominins are early Neanderthals, the nDNA data pushes the population divergence between Neanderthals and Denisovans to a time predating 430,000 years ago , , . Recalibrations based on this data suggest the Neanderthal–Denisovan split occurred around 450,000 years ago, and the split between the modern human lineage and the ancestor of archaic humans (Neanderthals/Denisovans) occurred around 650,000 years ago, with a proposed range of 550,000 to 750,000 years ago . These dates are now foundational in models of human origins. An alternative, more nuanced hypothesis has also been proposed to explain the anomaly: adaptive mitochondrial introgression . This model suggests that the ancestral Neanderthal mtDNA lineage may have accumulated deleterious mutations due to inefficient purifying selection in a small, isolated population like the one at Sima de los Huesos. A foreign, more "fit" mtDNA haplotype from an interbreeding event could then have replaced the original, dysfunctional one, a process that would leave the nuclear genome unchanged but alter the mitochondrial record . Regardless of the exact mechanism, the story of the Sima hominins demonstrates that archaic human populations were not static entities but were involved in complex interactions and gene flow events that profoundly shaped their evolutionary trajectories. The successful extraction of this ancient DNA, achieved through optimized methods designed to handle low endogenous DNA content and high contamination levels, stands as a testament to the power of technological innovation in paleoanthropology , .

## Taphonomy and Behavioral Interpretations

The manner in which the approximately 29 individuals of the Sima de los Huesos population came to be buried in the deep pit is a central question that lies at the intersection of geology, biology, and archaeology. The taphonomic evidence—the study of what happens to organisms after death—provides a complex and compelling narrative about the site's formation and offers tantalizing clues about the behavior of its creators. The primary depositional mechanism appears to have been passive, resulting from natural processes rather than deliberate construction. The geological context of the LU-6 breccia, as previously noted, lacks features indicative of water transport and instead shows patterns consistent with low-energy vertical falls and mudflows, strongly suggesting that bodies were deposited in the pit by falling down the 13-meter vertical shaft from above . This interpretation is supported by the absence of cut marks, burning, or other signs of cultural modification on the bones, as well as the limited number of carnivore tooth marks, which are sporadic and interpreted as having occurred after the individuals were already trapped in the chamber , . Therefore, the initial accumulation of the cadavers was likely an accident, a tragic consequence of the unstable nature of the cave environment.

However, the taphonomic signature goes beyond simple deposition and points toward a more deliberate process. A comprehensive analysis of the bone assemblage reveals a remarkable degree of completeness and representation. Virtually every anatomical part of the skeleton is present, and the bones show little sign of transport or disarticulation after burial, suggesting that whole bodies were placed in the site , . This contrasts sharply with other fossil assemblages, such as that of *Homo naledi* at Dinaledi, where carnivores appear to have played no role in accumulation . The lack of carnivore activity and the rapid sealing of the site by sediment support the hypothesis that the bodies were disposed of soon after death, preserving the skeletons in a collective burial-like context . This leads to the provocative interpretation that the Sima hominins engaged in intentional disposal of their dead, a practice that would represent one of the earliest claims for mortuary behavior in the human lineage , . The strongest piece of evidence cited in support of this hypothesis is the discovery of a single Acheulean-style handaxe, dubbed "Excalibur," in the southern part of the pit in 1998 , . This artifact is a well-made symmetrical biface, a tool associated with *Homo heidelbergensis*, and its recovery without any associated lithic waste flakes is unusual , . Some researchers have interpreted this find as a symbolic offering deliberately placed with the dead, a claim that, if validated, would push back the origins of symbolic thought and ritualistic behavior by hundreds of thousands of years .

The skeletal record of the Sima population also provides direct evidence of interpersonal violence, further complicating the picture of their behavior. A detailed forensic-taphonomic analysis of the crania has identified nine individuals with perimortem fractures—breaks that occurred around the time of death , . In six of these cases, the fractures are recurrent, circular, and penetrate the left nuchal region (the back of the head), a location that is anatomically improbable for accidental trauma , . The most famous example is Cranium 17, which displays two indistinguishable depressed fractures caused by repeated blows from a standardized tool, confirming lethal interpersonal violence , . CT-based analyses of other crania, such as Crania 5 and 11, also suggest that violence was a plausible explanation for their perimortem trauma . This body of evidence suggests that recurrent interpersonal violence was a feature of life in this Middle Pleistocene population, adding a dark chapter to the story of their existence . While some alternative explanations, such as attacks by cave bears, have been proposed for certain traumatic lesions, the pattern of recurrent, targeted violence seen in multiple individuals lends strong support to the interpretation of homicide , . The combination of evidence—from the intact, whole-body deposition to the controversial "Excalibur" artifact and the clear signs of lethal violence—paints a multifaceted portrait. It suggests a population that, while living in a harsh and dangerous world, may have developed complex social structures capable of both committing acts of violence and engaging in rituals that involved the deliberate and respectful disposal of their dead. Whether this represents the dawn of true mortuary practice or simply a pragmatic solution to disposing of cadavers in a treacherous landscape remains a topic of active scholarly debate, but the evidence from Sima de los Huesos undeniably challenges simplistic notions of Middle Pleistocene human cognition and behavior.

## Significance in Human Evolutionary Theory

The Sima de los Huesos hominins hold a monumental place in the field of paleoanthropology, serving as a cornerstone for understanding the origins and evolution of Neanderthals and the complex dynamics of archaic human populations. Their significance extends across multiple domains, from taxonomy and evolutionary modeling to genetics and behavioral archaeology. Perhaps their most profound contribution has been in clarifying the taxonomic and evolutionary trajectory of Neanderthals. Before the detailed study of the Sima assemblage, the Middle Pleistocene of Europe was a confusing patchwork of fossils, often lumped together under the paraphyletic genus *Homo heidelbergensis*. The overwhelming weight of evidence from Sima—spanning cranial, dental, and postcranial anatomy—has demonstrated that this population is unequivocally an early member of the Neanderthal clade, possessing a suite of derived Neanderthal traits , , . This has allowed researchers like Chris Stringer to argue persuasively that reclassifying the Sima hominins as early Neanderthals restores *Homo heidelbergensis* to its proper role as the last common ancestor of Neanderthals, Denisovans, and modern humans, resolving a long-standing taxonomic ambiguity .

Furthermore, the Sima fossils provide the strongest support to date for the "accretion model" of Neanderthal evolution , . This model proposes that the Neanderthal phenotype did not arise suddenly but evolved gradually through the stepwise addition of derived traits. The mosaic morphology of the Sima hominins perfectly exemplifies this process: they exhibit advanced Neanderthal-like features in their faces, jaws, and teeth, while retaining a more primitive, generalized braincase morphology , , . This pattern indicates that the dramatic changes to the midface and masticatory apparatus were among the earliest stages in the "neanderthalization" of the lineage, preceding the later evolution of the larger brains and reorganized braincases characteristic of classic Neanderthals , . The Sima population thus represents a crucial "missing link," capturing a stage in human evolution where the Neanderthal lineage was clearly established but had not yet reached its final, iconic form. This makes them a vital reference point for distinguishing between populations that are merely ancestral and those that are direct members of the Neanderthal lineage.

The genetic revelations from Sima de los Huesos have arguably been the most transformative aspect of the site's legacy. The discovery of mitonuclear discordance—where the mtDNA links them to Denisovans while the nDNA confirms their Neanderthal ancestry—provided the first direct molecular evidence of complex population interactions in the Middle Pleistocene , . This finding shattered the simple, tree-like model of human evolution and introduced a more dynamic, reticulate view where different lineages mixed and exchanged genes . It forced a re-evaluation of the timing of key divergence events, pushing the split between Neanderthals and Denisovans back into the Middle Pleistocene and cementing the importance of the Sima hominins as a population existing at this very moment of evolutionary divergence , . The successful extraction of the oldest nuclear genome from a non-permafrost context has opened a new frontier in ancient DNA research, proving that genetic information can survive for hundreds of thousands of years even in temperate climates, thereby expanding the scope of questions that can be asked about deep human history , .

In summary, the Sima de los Huesos hominins have fundamentally reshaped our understanding of human evolution. They have clarified the taxonomic status of a key European population, provided a textbook example of mosaic evolution, and unveiled the complex reality of archaic human population dynamics through the lens of ancient DNA. The site continues to be a focal point for high-precision geochronological research and ongoing taphonomic studies aimed at deciphering the behavioral motivations behind the accumulation of these remains , . The combination of an exceptionally large, well-preserved, and precisely dated fossil assemblage with a rich archaeological context ensures that the Pit of Bones will remain a central pillar of paleoanthropological inquiry for the foreseeable future, continually yielding new insights into the lives, deaths, and legacies of our closest extinct relatives.

The faunal association in the Sima de los Huesos chamber provides additional context.
The Sima de los Huesos chamber contains a vast number of bear bones, primarily from the extinct cave bear species *Ursus deningeri*.
The Sima de los Huesos chamber contains remains of other carnivores like the cave lion (*Panthera leo*) and wolf (*Canis lupus*).
Stratigraphic relationships suggest that the hominins were deposited before the bears in Sima de los Huesos.
The hominins and animals in Sima de los Huesos were possibly trapped inside when the upper shaft collapsed.
The precise dating of the Sima de los Huesos hominins has been a central focus of research and a source of considerable debate.
The dating of the Sima de los Huesos hominins ultimately led to a high-resolution chronology based on the convergence of multiple independent geochronological methods.
Early estimates placed the age of the Sima de los Huesos fossils between 400,000 and 500,000 years ago.
Some studies suggested a much older date of around 600,000 years for the Sima de los Huesos fossils.
A 2007 study by Bischoff et al. proposed an age of ~600 ka for Sima de los Huesos based on U-series dating.
The ~600 ka age proposed by Bischoff et al. for Sima de los Huesos was contested by others.
A series of more advanced and integrated dating techniques have progressively refined the Sima de los Huesos timeline, establishing a robust consensus.
A landmark 2014 study by Arsuaga et al. synthesized data from uranium-series (U-series) dating of speleothems that formed on top of the crania.

The 2014 study by Arsuaga et al. synthesized data from thermally transferred optically stimulated luminescence (TT-OSL) and post-infrared stimulated luminescence (pIR-IRSL) on quartz and feldspar grains within the sediment.
The 2014 study by Arsuaga et al. synthesized data from electron spin resonance (ESR) dating of fossil teeth and sedimentary quartz.
The 2014 study by Arsuaga et al. synthesized data from paleomagnetism.
The multi-pronged approach used in the 2014 study, analyzed using a Bayesian age-depth model, constrained the age of the LU-6 unit to approximately 430,000 years ago.
The refined range for the age of the LU-6 unit is 410,000 to 460,000 years ago.
This date for the LU-6 unit is now widely accepted and superseded earlier broader estimates.
The age places the Sima hominins squarely within Marine Isotope Stage (MIS) 12.
MIS 12 was a period of cool climate conditions.
This precise chronology is critical for understanding the Sima de los Huesos site itself.
The precise chronology of Sima de los Huesos has profound implications in human evolutionary theory.
The Sima de los Huesos chronology situates the population near the predicted time of the divergence between the Neanderthal and Denisovan lineages.
Uranium-Series (U-series) dating measures the decay of uranium isotopes in calcite deposits.
Uranium-Series (U-series) dating provided a minimum age of 410,000–460,000 years from calcite rafts on Cranium 4.
Thermally Transferred OSL (TT-OSL) / pIR-IRSL measures light emitted from mineral grains to determine last exposure to sunlight.
Thermally Transferred OSL (TT-OSL) / pIR-IRSL provided a maximum age of 448,000 ± 15,000 years from underlying red clay (LU-6).
Electron Spin Resonance (ESR) measures trapped electrons in tooth enamel and minerals.
ESR was used on fossil teeth and sedimentary quartz to provide multiple age points.
Paleomagnetism analyzes the magnetic polarity of sediment layers.
Paleomagnetism confirms LU-6 is younger than the Brunhes-Matuyama reversal (~780,000 years ago).
Bayesian Age-Depth Modeling integrates multiple age estimates to create a statistically robust chronological framework.
Bayesian Age-Depth Modeling constrained LU-6 to 430,000 years ago (range 410–460 ka).
The Sima de los Huesos fossil collection is extraordinary for its sheer volume, comprising over 7,000 individual bone fragments.
The Sima de los Huesos fossil collection is extraordinary for the remarkable completeness and quality of preservation of the material.
The Sima de los Huesos material has enabled an unprecedentedly detailed reconstruction of a single, cohesive Middle Pleistocene human population.
The Sima de los Huesos assemblage includes representatives of virtually all anatomical parts, from complete distal pedal phalanges to fragmentary skulls and postcranial elements.
The Sima de los Huesos assemblage allows for comprehensive morphological and biological analyses.
As of the latest assessments, the Sima de los Huesos collection represents a minimum of 29 individuals.
The estimate of 29 individuals is an update from the previous estimate of 28.

The figure of 29 individuals is based on extensive dentognathic reconstruction, including antimeric fitting of jaw fragments, staging of occlusal wear, and analysis of developmental markers like enamel hypoplasia.
The dentognathic reconstruction accounts for damage inflicted by amateur cavers prior to formal excavation.
The sex ratio of the Sima de los Huesos population is not significantly different from a 1:1 balance.
The finding of a 1:1 sex ratio corrects earlier suggestions of female predominance in the Sima de los Huesos population.
The Sima de los Huesos remains span a wide range of ages, from preadolescents to individuals reaching advanced age.
The Sima de los Huesos remains provide a rare snapshot of a closed-population demography.
A detailed analysis of the age-at-death distribution in Sima de los Huesos reveals a striking mortality profile, often described as "catastrophic" or L-shaped.
The Sima de los Huesos mortality profile indicates a skewed population structure.
Among the 29 individuals from Sima de los Huesos, 12 were immature (41.4%).
Another 12 individuals from Sima de los Huesos were young adults (aged approximately 17–30 years, 41.4%).
Only 4 middle-aged adults (13.8%) were found among the 29 individuals from Sima de los Huesos.
This pattern suggests a population with a high rate of mortality among the young and a scarcity of individuals surviving to middle age.
Further analysis of dental development in Sima de los Huesos shows a significant acceleration compared to modern humans.
Third molar (wisdom tooth) eruption in Sima de los Huesos hominins occurred systematically 2.8 to 4.1 years earlier than in modern humans.
The average age of third molar eruption in Sima de los Huesos hominins is estimated at 14–15 years.
The average age of third molar eruption in contemporary human populations is approximately 18 years.
This accelerated maturation is a distinctive feature of the Sima hominins.
Accelerated maturation provides a key biochronological marker for identifying members of this population across different archaeological contexts.
Over 7,500 total fossils were recovered from Sima de los Huesos.
The Estimated Number of Individuals (ENI) from Sima de los Huesos is 29 (updated from 28).
The Age-at-Death Distribution for Sima de los Huesos is 41.4% Immature, 41.4% Young Adult, 13.8% Middle-Aged Adult.
Accelerated Third Molar Development in Sima de los Huesos hominins is systematically advanced by 2.8–4.1 years vs. modern humans.
The Sex Ratio of the Sima de los Huesos population is not significantly different from 1:1.
Nearly all anatomical parts are represented in the Sima de los Huesos collection, including complete distal pedal phalanges.
The Sima de los Huesos hominins' overall body plan is characterized by robustness and a "wide" bauplan.
The "wide" bauplan is a plesiomorphic trait inherited from early hominin ancestors.
Stature estimates for the Sima de los Huesos population are comparable to those of modern human middle-latitude populations.
Mean statures for the Sima de los Huesos population are calculated at 174.4 cm for males and 161.9 cm for females based on talar measurements.
Long-bone-based estimates confirm these robust modern human-like body proportions for Sima de los Huesos hominins.
Despite some gracility, the Sima de los Huesos population exhibited a highly robust body plan overall.
The robust body plan of Sima de los Huesos hominins contrasts sharply with the more gracile build of modern humans.
Robust features in Sima de los Huesos hominins are evident in broad pelves, long superior pubic rami, and broad lumbar transverse processes.
Body mass of Sima de los Huesos hominins was slightly lower than that of later Neanderthals.
The encephalization quotient (EQ) of Sima de los Huesos hominins, a measure of relative brain size, was significantly lower than both Neanderthals and modern humans.
The lower EQ of Sima de los Huesos hominins suggests that full Neanderthal-sized brains had not yet evolved in this population.
This mosaic pattern of traits highlights the stepwise nature of Neanderthal evolution.
Perhaps the most poignant aspect of the Sima de los Huesos collection is the evidence of pathology and potential care for the infirm.
One of the most remarkable discoveries at Sima de los Huesos is Cranium 14, the skull of an immature individual aged between 5 and 12.5 years at death.
Cranium 14 suffered from severe lambdoid single suture craniosynostosis, a congenital condition where the lambdoid sutures of the skull fuse prematurely.
Lambdoid single suture craniosynostosis causes severe deformity of the head and likely associated cognitive and motor disorders.
The severity of the deformity in Cranium 14, including pronounced cribra orbitalia (porous lesions on the eye sockets), was the most extreme seen in the entire Sima sample.
The survival of the individual with Cranium 14 to a relatively advanced age implies that they received care from their conspecifics.
The survival of the individual with Cranium 14 offers a rare and powerful glimpse into the potential for compassion and social support within this Middle Pleistocene community.
Another compelling case of pathological stress in Sima de los Huesos is found in the form of widespread healed antemortem cranial injuries.
A comprehensive taphonomic study identified 57 distinct, circular, blunt-force trauma lesions across 17 of the 20 crania analyzed from Sima de los Huesos.
These lesions show clear signs of bone remodeling and healing.
The healed lesions affected individuals of all ages and both sexes, indicating that the entire Sima de los Huesos population was exposed to recurrent, nonfatal cranial impacts throughout their lives.
While the cause of these injuries is debated, interpretations range from accidental hazards of daily life to recurrent low-level interpersonal violence.
The presence of such a high frequency of healed injuries paints a picture of a challenging and potentially violent existence for these ancient people.
The taxonomic placement of the Sima de los Huesos hominins has been a subject of intense scholarly debate.
The taxonomic placement of the Sima de los Huesos hominins fundamentally reshaped the understanding of human evolution in Europe during the Middle Pleistocene.
For decades, fossils from the Middle Pleistocene era, including those from Sima de los Huesos, were broadly classified under the species *Homo heidelbergensis*.
*Homo heidelbergensis* was envisioned as the last common ancestor of Neanderthals, Denisovans, and modern humans.
The wealth of new data from Atapuerca, combined with discoveries elsewhere, has led to a significant re-evaluation of hominin classification.
The overwhelming consensus from morphological and genetic analyses is that the Sima hominins are best classified as early members of the Neanderthal lineage, rather than as *H. heidelbergensis*.

This conclusion is supported by a suite of derived traits that align Sima hominins more closely with classic Neanderthals than with contemporaneous or earlier hominins like *Homo erectus* or *Homo naledi*.
The shift in classification was catalyzed by molecular divergence estimates that pointed to a split between Neanderthals and modern humans around 400,000 years ago.
The 400,000 years ago timeframe coincided with the age of the Sima fossils.
The coincidence of the split timeframe with the age of Sima fossils made it difficult to place them within a basal *H. heidelbergensis* group.
Detailed anatomical analysis of the Sima crania provides strong evidence for their status as basal Neanderthals.
One of the most definitive pieces of evidence comes from the morphology of the bony labyrinth (inner ear).
Studies have shown that the semicircular canal proportions of the Sima hominins exhibit a derived pattern identical to that of Neanderthals.
The derived pattern in Sima hominins includes a relatively smaller posterior canal and a relatively larger lateral canal.
The semicircular canal pattern in Sima hominins is distinct from the pattern seen in *Homo sapiens*, *H. ergaster/erectus*, and early hominins.
Furthermore, the SH bony labyrinth is considered primitive relative to later Neanderthals.
The SH bony labyrinth lacks certain derived features like a high sagittal labyrinthine index.
The primitive nature of the SH bony labyrinth confirms their position as basal members of the Neanderthal clade rather than as *H. heidelbergensis*.
Cranially, the Sima sample exhibits a characteristic mosaic of traits.
Sima hominins possess several derived Neanderthal features, particularly in the face and anterior vault, related to the masticatory apparatus.
These features include intensive frontal tooth wear, which suggests the use of the mouth as a 'third hand' for holding objects while working.
The supraorbital torus (brow ridge) of Sima hominins is thick and torsioned.
A thick and torsioned supraorbital torus is a feature also seen in early Neanderthals.
The supraorbital torus of Sima hominins lacks the fully arched profile of classic Neanderthals.
The braincase morphology of Sima hominins retains more primitive characteristics.
The primitive braincase morphology supports the "accretion model" of Neanderthal evolution.
The accretion model posits that facial modifications preceded significant changes in the neurocranium.
Endocranial volumes of Sima hominins vary considerably, with specimens ranging from 1,125 cm³ to 1,390 cm³.
The average endocranial volume of Sima hominins is around 1,232 cm³.
The average endocranial volume of Sima hominins is less derived than the larger brains of later Neanderthals.
The dental remains from Sima de los Huesos constitute the largest Middle Pleistocene hominin dental assemblage ever recovered, comprising over 533 teeth.
The extensive dental sample from Sima de los Huesos allows for a nuanced understanding of their dental evolution.
The molars of Sima de los Huesos hominins exhibit "almost morphological identity with European Neanderthals."
Sima de los Huesos molars display a high frequency of taurodontism (enlarged pulp chambers), with a prevalence of approximately 75%.
The high frequency of taurodontism links this Middle Pleistocene population morphologically to later Neanderthals.
The occlusal patterns of the upper first molars (M1s) in Sima de los Huesos show a mosaic of traits.
Some features of the M1s in Sima de los Huesos match *Homo neanderthalensis* while others align with *Homo sapiens*.
This mosaic pattern highlights the complexity of dental evolution and cautions against simplistic taxonomic assignments based on isolated teeth.

While the absolute and relative enamel thickness of SH molars is generally thick and plesiomorphic (primitive), similar to that of *Homo erectus* and modern humans, the enamel distribution pattern is derived and Neanderthal-like.
The derived enamel distribution pattern in SH molars shows thicker enamel concentrated on the lingual cusps.
This dual signal—retaining ancestral enamel thickness while evolving a derived distribution—is a key piece of evidence supporting their position as early Neanderthals.
A 2025 study further complicates the picture by noting intrapopulation variability in enamel thickness.
The 2025 study cautions against relying solely on enamel thickness for taxonomy.
Lower premolars in Sima de los Huesos show a more modern-human-like pattern while upper premolars are more Neanderthal-like.
Postcranially, the Sima hominins display a similarly mosaic pattern of Neanderthal apomorphies and primitive traits.
The talus (ankle bone) is a key element of interest in Sima de los Huesos hominins.
The Sima de los Huesos sample includes 17 talus specimens.
All 17 talus specimens show complete fusion of the anterior and middle calcaneal articular surfaces.
Complete fusion of the anterior and middle calcaneal articular surfaces is an autapomorphic trait shared with Neanderthals (present in 96% of the sample).
The complete fusion of articular surfaces is less common in both Pleistocene and recent *Homo sapiens* (present in 88.9% and 55-75% respectively).
The SH tali are vertically shorter and have a broader lateral malleolar facet than all comparative samples.
The SH tali contribute to a broader, more robust foot morphology.
Other postcranial elements, such as the pelvis, also show features consistent with the Neanderthal clade.
Pelvic features consistent with the Neanderthal clade include a broad elliptical shape with a wide sacrum and long pubic rami.
The Sima de los Huesos population also retains primitive traits, such as large femoral heads.
Large femoral heads are characteristic of the Middle Pleistocene.
This mosaic evolution in the postcranium underscores the gradual and piecemeal nature of the transition to the classic Neanderthal phenotype.
The combination of cranial, dental, and postcranial features solidifies the classification of the Sima de los Huesos hominins as a pivotal link in the evolutionary chain leading to Neanderthals.
The advent of ancient DNA (aDNA) technology has revolutionized the study of the Sima de los Huesos hominins.
Ancient DNA technology introduced a profound paradox that has become central to modern discussions of archaic human evolution.
In 2014, a groundbreaking study published in *Nature* successfully sequenced mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) from a 400,000-year-old femur from the Sima de los Huesos site.
The sequenced mtDNA from Sima de los Huesos represented the oldest hominin genetic material ever retrieved at the time.
The results of the 2014 study were astonishing: the mtDNA from the Sima hominin formed a clade with the Denisovan lineage.
The Denisovan lineage is an archaic human group known primarily from fossils found in Siberia.
The Sima hominin mtDNA was more distantly related to Neanderthals.
This finding was deeply contradictory because the skeletal anatomy of the Sima fossils is unambiguously Neanderthal-like.
The Sima fossils exhibit numerous derived traits that are hallmarks of the Neanderthal lineage.
This discrepancy, known as mitonuclear discordance, presented a major puzzle: how could a population with Neanderthal-like bones carry Denisovan-like mtDNA?
The initial surprise was compounded by the fact that the Sima hominins were dated to approximately 430,000 years ago.
The dating of Sima hominins placed them at a critical juncture in human evolution, near the hypothesized time of the Neanderthal-Denisovan split.
To resolve this enigma, scientists turned to the even more challenging task of extracting ancient nuclear DNA (nDNA).
Nuclear DNA carries the vast majority of an organism's genetic information and provides a more reliable phylogenetic signal.
In 2016, another landmark study, also published in *Nature*, announced the successful retrieval and sequencing of nDNA from two Sima hominin specimens.
The results of the nDNA analysis were definitive: the Sima hominins are indeed part of the Neanderthal evolutionary lineage.
The Sima hominins show a closer phylogenetic relationship to Neanderthals than to Denisovans.
This finding resolved the paradox by demonstrating that the surprising mtDNA result did not represent the ancestral state of the population but rather a subsequent event in their history.

The scientific consensus that emerged from this research is that the Sima population, while belonging to the early Neanderthal lineage, must have experienced gene flow from another archaic hominin group.
The gene flow likely came from a group related to Denisovans or perhaps an unknown population.
The gene flow introduced the Denisovan-like mtDNA lineage into their gene pool.
This later mtDNA replacement event explains why the maternal lineages diverged from the main Neanderthal branch before the split between Neanderthals and Denisovans.
The rest of the Sima hominins' genome remained firmly rooted in the Neanderthal clade.
This mitonuclear discordance has had far-reaching implications for calibrating the timelines of human evolution.
By confirming that the Sima hominins are early Neanderthals, the nDNA data pushes the population divergence between Neanderthals and Denisovans to a time predating 430,000 years ago.
Recalibrations based on this data suggest the Neanderthal–Denisovan split occurred around 450,000 years ago.
The split between the modern human lineage and the ancestor of archaic humans (Neanderthals/Denisovans) occurred around 650,000 years ago.
A proposed range for the split between the modern human lineage and the ancestor of archaic humans is 550,000 to 750,000 years ago.
These dates are now foundational in models of human origins.
An alternative, more nuanced hypothesis has also been proposed to explain the anomaly: adaptive mitochondrial introgression.

The adaptive mitochondrial introgression model suggests that the ancestral Neanderthal mtDNA lineage may have accumulated deleterious mutations due to inefficient purifying selection in a small, isolated population like the one at Sima de los Huesos.
A foreign, more "fit" mtDNA haplotype from an interbreeding event could then have replaced the original, dysfunctional one.
The process of adaptive mitochondrial introgression would leave the nuclear genome unchanged but alter the mitochondrial record.
The story of the Sima hominins demonstrates that archaic human populations were not static entities.
Archaic human populations were involved in complex interactions and gene flow events that profoundly shaped their evolutionary trajectories.

The successful extraction of this ancient DNA, achieved through optimized methods designed to handle low endogenous DNA content and high contamination levels, stands as a testament to the power of technological innovation in paleoanthropology.
Mitochondrial DNA (2014) from Sima de los Huesos clusters with Denisovans, not Neanderthals.
The mitochondrial DNA finding creates a paradox given the Neanderthal-like anatomy of Sima de los Huesos hominins.
Nuclear DNA (2016) confirms phylogenetic placement within the Neanderthal lineage for Sima de los Huesos hominins.
Sima de los Huesos hominins are more closely related to Neanderthals than to Denisovans.
The nuclear DNA finding resolves the mitonuclear paradox.
The interpretation of discordance suggests a later gene flow event (introgression) from a Denisovan-related or unknown archaic population into the early Neanderthal lineage.
The impact on divergence timelines pushes the Neanderthal-Denisovan split to before ~430,000 years ago.
The impact on divergence timelines pushes the modern human-archaic split to ~650,000 years ago.

The manner in which the approximately 29 individuals of the Sima de los Huesos population came to be buried in the deep pit is a central question that lies at the intersection of geology, biology, and archaeology.
The taphonomic evidence provides a complex and compelling narrative about the Sima de los Huesos site's formation.
The taphonomic evidence offers tantalizing clues about the behavior of its creators.
The primary depositional mechanism at Sima de los Huesos appears to have been passive, resulting from natural processes rather than deliberate construction.
The geological context of the LU-6 breccia lacks features indicative of water transport.
The LU-6 breccia instead shows patterns consistent with low-energy vertical falls and mudflows.
The patterns in the LU-6 breccia strongly suggest that bodies were deposited in the pit by falling down the 13-meter vertical shaft from above.
This interpretation is supported by the absence of cut marks, burning, or other signs of cultural modification on the bones.
The interpretation is also supported by the limited number of carnivore tooth marks, which are sporadic and interpreted as having occurred after the individuals were already trapped in the chamber.
Therefore, the initial accumulation of the cadavers at Sima de los Huesos was likely an accident, a tragic consequence of the unstable nature of the cave environment.
However, the taphonomic signature goes beyond simple deposition and points toward a more deliberate process.
A comprehensive analysis of the Sima de los Huesos bone assemblage reveals a remarkable degree of completeness and representation.
Virtually every anatomical part of the skeleton is present in Sima de los Huesos.
The bones show little sign of transport or disarticulation after burial, suggesting that whole bodies were placed in the Sima de los Huesos site.
This contrasts sharply with other fossil assemblages, such as that of *Homo naledi* at Dinaledi, where carnivores appear to have played no role in accumulation.
The lack of carnivore activity and the rapid sealing of the Sima de los Huesos site by sediment support the hypothesis that the bodies were disposed of soon after death.
The rapid sealing of the Sima de los Huesos site by sediment preserved the skeletons in a collective burial-like context.
This leads to the provocative interpretation that the Sima hominins engaged in intentional disposal of their dead.
Intentional disposal of the dead would represent one of the earliest claims for mortuary behavior in the human lineage.

The strongest piece of evidence cited in support of this hypothesis is the discovery of a single Acheulean-style handaxe, dubbed "Excalibur," in the southern part of the Sima de los Huesos pit in 1998.
The "Excalibur" artifact is a well-made symmetrical biface, a tool associated with *Homo heidelbergensis*.
Its recovery without any associated lithic waste flakes is unusual.
Some researchers have interpreted this find as a symbolic offering deliberately placed with the dead.
If validated, the interpretation of "Excalibur" as a symbolic offering would push back the origins of symbolic thought and ritualistic behavior by hundreds of thousands of years.
The skeletal record of the Sima population also provides direct evidence of interpersonal violence.
A detailed forensic-taphonomic analysis of the crania has identified nine individuals with perimortem fractures—breaks that occurred around the time of death.
In six of these cases, the fractures are recurrent, circular, and penetrate the left nuchal region (the back of the head).
The location of the fractures in the left nuchal region is anatomically improbable for accidental trauma.
The most famous example is Cranium 17, which displays two indistinguishable depressed fractures caused by repeated blows from a standardized tool.
The fractures on Cranium 17 confirm lethal interpersonal violence.
CT-based analyses of other crania, such as Crania 5 and 11, also suggest that violence was a plausible explanation for their perimortem trauma.
This body of evidence suggests that recurrent interpersonal violence was a feature of life in this Middle Pleistocene population.
Recurrent interpersonal violence adds a dark chapter to the story of their existence.

While some alternative explanations, such as attacks by cave bears, have been proposed for certain traumatic lesions, the pattern of recurrent, targeted violence seen in multiple individuals lends strong support to the interpretation of homicide.
The combination of evidence from Sima de los Huesos suggests a population that, while living in a harsh and dangerous world, may have developed complex social structures.

The Sima de los Huesos population's complex social structures were capable of both committing acts of violence and engaging in rituals that involved the deliberate and respectful disposal of their dead.
The Sima de los Huesos hominins hold a monumental place in the field of paleoanthropology.
The Sima de los Huesos hominins serve as a cornerstone for understanding the origins and evolution of Neanderthals and the complex dynamics of archaic human populations.
Their significance extends across multiple domains, from taxonomy and evolutionary modeling to genetics and behavioral archaeology.
Perhaps their most profound contribution has been in clarifying the taxonomic and evolutionary trajectory of Neanderthals.
Before the detailed study of the Sima assemblage, the Middle Pleistocene of Europe was a confusing patchwork of fossils, often lumped together under the paraphyletic genus *Homo heidelbergensis*.
The overwhelming weight of evidence from Sima—spanning cranial, dental, and postcranial anatomy—has demonstrated that this population is unequivocally an early member of the Neanderthal clade.
The Sima population possesses a suite of derived Neanderthal traits.

This has allowed researchers like Chris Stringer to argue persuasively that reclassifying the Sima hominins as early Neanderthals restores *Homo heidelbergensis* to its proper role as the last common ancestor of Neanderthals, Denisovans, and modern humans.
Reclassifying the Sima hominins as early Neanderthals resolves a long-standing taxonomic ambiguity.
Furthermore, the Sima fossils provide the strongest support to date for the "accretion model" of Neanderthal evolution.
The accretion model proposes that the Neanderthal phenotype did not arise suddenly but evolved gradually through the stepwise addition of derived traits.
The mosaic morphology of the Sima hominins perfectly exemplifies this process.
Sima hominins exhibit advanced Neanderthal-like features in their faces, jaws, and teeth.
Sima hominins retain a more primitive, generalized braincase morphology.
This pattern indicates that the dramatic changes to the midface and masticatory apparatus were among the earliest stages in the "neanderthalization" of the lineage.
The changes to the midface and masticatory apparatus preceded the later evolution of the larger brains and reorganized braincases characteristic of classic Neanderthals.

The Sima population thus represents a crucial "missing link," capturing a stage in human evolution where the Neanderthal lineage was clearly established but had not yet reached its final, iconic form.
This makes them a vital reference point for distinguishing between populations that are merely ancestral and those that are direct members of the Neanderthal lineage.
The genetic revelations from Sima de los Huesos have arguably been the most transformative aspect of the site's legacy.

The discovery of mitonuclear discordance—where the mtDNA links them to Denisovans while the nDNA confirms their Neanderthal ancestry—provided the first direct molecular evidence of complex population interactions in the Middle Pleistocene.
This finding shattered the simple, tree-like model of human evolution and introduced a more dynamic, reticulate view where different lineages mixed and exchanged genes.
It forced a re-evaluation of the timing of key divergence events.
The re-evaluation pushed the split between Neanderthals and Denisovans back into the Middle Pleistocene.
The re-evaluation cemented the importance of the Sima hominins as a population existing at this very moment of evolutionary divergence.
The successful extraction of the oldest nuclear genome from a non-permafrost context has opened a new frontier in ancient DNA research.
The successful extraction proved that genetic information can survive for hundreds of thousands of years even in temperate climates.
The successful extraction expanded the scope of questions that can be asked about deep human history.
The Sima de los Huesos hominins have fundamentally reshaped our understanding of human evolution.
They have clarified the taxonomic status of a key European population.
They have provided a textbook example of mosaic evolution.
They have unveiled the complex reality of archaic human population dynamics through the lens of ancient DNA.
The Sima de los Huesos site continues to be a focal point for high-precision geochronological research.
The Sima de los Huesos site continues to be a focal point for ongoing taphonomic studies aimed at deciphering the behavioral motivations behind the accumulation of these remains.

The combination of an exceptionally large, well-preserved, and precisely dated fossil assemblage with a rich archaeological context ensures that the Pit of Bones will remain a central pillar of paleoanthropological inquiry for the foreseeable future.
The Pit of Bones will continually yield new insights into the lives, deaths, and legacies of our closest extinct relatives.

Abstract
--------

After 34 years of research and findings in the Middle Pleistocene site of the Sima de los Huesos (SH) of the Sierra de Atapuerca (Burgos, Spain), we present an update of the estimation of the number of individuals (ENI) identified in the SH hominin assemblage. The last ENI, published in 2004, was 28. Although the number of specimens recovered has almost doubled since then and more complete information is now available, this new analysis suggests that the ENI is 29. Some individuals are still represented by only one or a few teeth and the upper and lower jaws of various individuals have not been completed. We suggest that the amateur cavers, who accessed the SH site for years looking for bear fossils, destroyed a significant number of hominin fossils. Despite this, we have a good picture of the group of hominins represented in the SH assemblage. Because complete corpses were accumulated in SH and it is a closed cavity, it is expected that a significant number of hominin fossils remains to be discovered. According to the previous estimates, the representation of females is greater than that of males. However, the observed sex ratio is not significantly different from the 1:1 ratio. With the exception of the possible presence of a child individual, most of the remaining 28 individuals are teenagers or young adults (24/28 = 0.857). The ages of death of SH hominins appear to conform to a catastrophic profile.

**Keywords:** Sierra de Atapuerca; Sima de los Huesos; age at death; hominins; number of individuals; sex.

Abstract
--------

Previous studies of upper first molar (M1) crown shape have shown significant differences between _Homo sapiens_ and _Homo neanderthalensis_ that were already present in the European Middle Pleistocene populations, including the large dental sample from Atapuerca-Sima de los Huesos (SH). Analysis of other M1 features such as the total crown base area, cusp proportions, cusp angles and occlusal polygon have confirmed the differences between both lineages, becoming a useful tool for the taxonomic assignment of isolated teeth from Late Pleistocene sites. However, until now the pattern of expression of these variables has not been known for the SH sample. This fossil sample, the largest collection from the European Middle Pleistocene, is generally interpreted as being from the direct ancestors of Neanderthals, and thus is a reference sample for assessing the origin of the Neanderthal morphologies. Surprisingly, our study reveals that SH M1s present a unique mosaic of _H. neanderthalensis_ and _H. sapiens_ features. Regarding the cusp angles and the relative occlusal polygon area, SH matches the _H. neanderthalensis_ pattern. However, regarding the total crown base area and relative cusps size, SH M1s are similar to _H. sapiens_, with a small crown area, a strong hypocone reduction and a protocone enlargement, although the protocone expansion in SH is significantly larger than in any other group studied. The SH dental sample calls into question the uniqueness of some so-called modern traits. Our study also sounds a note of caution on the use of M1 occlusal morphology for the alpha taxonomy of isolated M1s.

**Keywords:** Atapuerca, cusp angle, cusp area, dental reduction, metrics, occusal polygon area, Sima de los Huesos, teeth

Introduction
------------

Previous analyses on the shape and metric features of M1s in the genus _Homo_ have revealed significant differences between _Homo sapiens_ and _Homo neanderthalensis_ lineages (Bailey, [2002a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b5), [2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b7); Bermúdez de Castro et al. [2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b16); Gómez-Robles et al. [2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b27), [2011a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b30); Quam et al. [2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b68)). Since M1 is considered to be the least variable and most diagnostic of the upper molars (Dahlberg, [1945](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b23); Bailey, [2002b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b6); Hlusko et al. [2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b39)), its anatomical details are expected to reflect the underlying genetic signal more strongly and thus it potentially provides evolutionary information. This circumstance is of particular utility for the taxonomic identification of isolated teeth (e.g. Smith, [1976](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b71); Morris, [1986](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b66); Wood et al. [1988](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b80); Klein, [1999](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b49); Tattersall, [1999](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b74); Bailey, [2002a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b5), [2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b7); Harvati et al. [2003](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b37)). Typical Neanderthal M1s have been described as strongly skewed rhomboids with bulging and protruding hypocones (Bailey, [2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b7)). This morphotype has been also identified in the European Early and Middle Pleistocene populations (Bailey, [2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b7); Quam et al. [2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b68)), including the large European Middle Pleistocene sample from Atapuerca-Sima de los Huesos (SH) (Gómez-Robles et al. [2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b27), [2011a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b30)), confirming the early appearance of some so-called Neanderthal features in Europe (Gómez-Robles et al. [2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b27), [2011a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b30); Martinón-Torres et al. [2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b58), [2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b60)). In addition, the pattern of expression of other typical Neanderthal M1 features such as the relative cusp proportions (e.g. a small metacone and large hypocone) or the small size of the relative occlusal polygon has been also identified in the small _Homo heidelbergensis_ sample analyzed by Bailey ([2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b7)) and Quam et al. ([2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b68)). However, to date, the pattern of expression of these features was unknown for the SH collection. The SH sample is currently the largest hominin collection worldwide for the Middle Pleistocene and provides an exceptional opportunity to study intra-population variability (e.g. Arsuaga et al. [1997a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b3); Lorenzo et al. [1998](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b54); Bermúdez de Castro et al. [2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b15); Gómez-Olivencia et al. [2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b25); Gómez-Robles et al. [2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b28), [2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b29), [2011b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b31),[c](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b32); Prado-Simón et al. [2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b67)). This hominin population has been assigned to _H. heidelbergensis_, assuming the latter to be a chronospecies of the European Neanderthal lineage (Arsuaga et al. [1991](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b1), [1993](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b2), [1997b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b4)). However, the precise relationship of the SH hominins with the Neanderthal lineage is still under debate (e.g. Stringer, [1993](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b72); Tattersall & Schwartz, [2006](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b75), [2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b76); Hublin, [2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b42)). On dental grounds, the SH hominins present all of the morphological traits that are usually considered typical of _H. neanderthalensis_ (Bermúdez de Castro, [1988](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b9), [1993](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b10); Martinón-Torres et al. [2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b60)), although in some features they appear even more derived than classic Neanderthals (Bermúdez de Castro & Nicolás, [1995](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b12), [1996](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b13); Gómez-Robles et al. [2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b27), [2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b28), [2011a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b30),[b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b31), [2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b33); Prado-Simón et al. [2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b67); Martinón-Torres et al. [2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b61)). In this context, it could be expected that SH M1s would also coincide with _H. neanderthalensis_ in their pattern of cusp proportions, cusp angles, occlusal polygon and crown size. In this study, we aim to contribute to the understanding of the evolution of M1 morphology by studying these features in the SH M1 sample.

Materials and methods
---------------------

Teeth with a wear degree higher than category 3 (Molnar, [1971](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b63)) were excluded from the SH M1 sample (_n_ = 29; Martinón-Torres et al. [2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b60)), resulting in a sample of 16 M1s. When antimeres were present, the data from the right side were used, resulting in a minimum number of 12 individuals (AT-20, AT-26, AT-139, AT-196, AT-587, AT-812, AT-959, AT-2076, AT-3177, AT-3178, AT-4317, AT-5899). The SH results were compared with data from other _Homo_ fossil and modern human samples obtained from the published literature. [Tables 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#tbl1) and [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#tbl2) list the specimens and source of the M1 comparative sample. The _H. heidelbergensis_ sample does not include the SH specimens, which are analyzed and compared separately. Measurements were taken by one of us (P.S.). For that purpose we employed standardized images of the occlusal surface of the molars. Photographs were taken with a Nikon D1H digital camera fitted with an AF Micro-Nikkor 105 mm, f/2.8D attached to a Kaiser Copy Stand kit RS-1 with grid baseboard, column, and adjustable camera arm. For maximum depth of field, we used an aperture of f/32, and the magnification ratio was adjusted to 1 : 1. A scale was placed parallel to and at the same distance from the lens as the occlusal plane. Images were measured with fiji image analysis software (Schindlein et al. [2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b70)). Each picture was calibrated three times and, following Bailey ([2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b7)), we used the average of these calibrations as the final calibration, and set a scale bar in the picture.

We measured the crown base area, individual cusp base areas, cusp angles and occlusal polygon area. We followed the methodology already employed by other authors in similar studies (Wood & Engleman, [1988](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b79); Bailey, [2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b7); Moggi-Cecchi & Boccone, [2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b62); Quam et al. [2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b68); Gómez-Robles et al. [2011a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b30)). We first traced the tooth perimeter. Individual cusp base areas were measured by following the primary fissures separating the cusps ([Fig. 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#fig01)). If the fissure was partially obscured, its course was estimated following the direction of the visible part of fissure (Bailey, [2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b7)) and with the help of other dental features as anatomical reference (Biggerstaff, [1969](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b19)). When necessary, the correction of interproximal wear was made according to Wood & Engleman ([1988](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b79)). When the metaconule or C5 was present, its area was measured and divided evenly between the adjacent main cusps (Quam et al. [2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b68); Gómez-Robles et al. [2011a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b30)). When a _crista obliqua_ was present we followed the recommendations of previous authors and continued the course of the central groove between the protocone and the metacone (Gómez-Robles et al. [2011a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3791128/#b30)). Cusps were considered equal in size if their relative areas did not differ by more than 1.0%. Total crown base area (TCBA) was calculated as the sum of individual cusp areas. Relative areas of each cusp were calculated by dividing the base area of each cusp by the total crown base area.
